Edge.long:
Edge, precisely, is a repeatable positive expectancy after every cost that trading actually incurs — commission, spread, slippage, financing. It is a claim about a process, not a description of a result: a strategy that made money once does not yet have an edge, it has a data point.

An edge needs a reason to exist. Genuine edges trace back to compensation for a risk others avoid, a structural constraint on some market participant, or a behavioural bias that is expensive for others to correct. Without one of those, a profitable-looking pattern is noise that arrived first.

Because it is a claim about a process, an edge is only as credible as the test that found it. A single backtest cannot distinguish a real edge from the best result of an unrecorded search — the same number means different things depending on how many variants were tried to reach it.

Where people get fooled: profitability in one sample gets treated as the discovery itself, when it is only ever the starting point for asking why the effect might exist and whether it survives the next dataset, the next regime, and the cost model that will actually apply.
Edge.usage: Used to separate a claimed cause for outperformance from the outperformance itself; a result earns the label only once a mechanism and an out-of-sample test both support it.

Backtest.long:
A backtest simulates how a strategy's rules would have performed against historical data — a rule set applied mechanically to the past to produce hypothetical trades. Its value is conditional on being an honest simulation of decisions the strategy could actually have made at the time, using only information available then.

The mechanism that breaks it is contact with the future. A backtest that uses adjusted prices without accounting for timing, restates the universe with hindsight by keeping only survivors, or lets a rule reference data not yet published, is testing a strategy that never existed. Clean code can still produce fiction.

A backtest is also one data point about how a rule set behaved on one historical path. A different sequence of the same underlying events could easily have produced a different verdict, which is why a single run earns provisional trust at best.

Where people get fooled: a clean equity curve reads as proof, but a backtest only ever answers what this rule would have produced on this exact history — it says nothing directly about tomorrow, and nothing about whether the rule was shaped by the history it is now being scored against.
Backtest.usage: The starting point for evaluating any rule-based idea, read as a conditional simulation rather than a track record, and never trusted from a single run.

Forward test.long:
A forward test runs a strategy's rules on data that arrives after the rules were fixed — genuinely new bars the strategy has never seen and could not have been tuned against, even unconsciously. It is the closest a backtest can get to a live trial without risking capital.

The mechanism it defends against is contamination through iteration. Historical out-of-sample data can quietly become in-sample the moment it is examined and reacted to; new data arriving after the rules are locked cannot, because it did not exist yet when the strategy was built.

Its cost is time and patience. A forward test only accumulates evidence at the rate the market produces new bars, so a strategy with a low trade frequency needs a long forward window before the result carries much statistical weight — there is no honest way to accelerate it.

Where people get fooled: a short, favourable forward-test stretch gets treated as confirmation, when a handful of trades on fresh data commands the same scepticism as a handful of trades anywhere else — it reduces contamination, it does not by itself supply sample size.
Forward test.usage: Run after a strategy's rules are frozen, on data that did not exist during development, to check whether performance survives contact with genuinely unseen bars.

Walk-forward.long:
Walk-forward testing splits history into successive windows: fit or select parameters on one stretch, test unchanged on the stretch immediately after, then roll both windows forward and repeat. Every test window is out-of-sample relative to the fit that preceded it, but the whole history eventually gets tested.

The mechanism it targets is a single lucky in-sample and out-of-sample split. One fixed cut can happen to land a strategy's strong or weak stretch on the wrong side by chance; walking the split across many positions checks whether performance holds up under a whole sequence of them rather than one.

It is not immune to leakage. If the fitting step is allowed to see anything from the test window — through overlapping labels, indicators with long lookbacks that straddle the boundary, or a researcher rerunning the whole process after seeing combined results — the walk-forward structure stops doing its job.

Where people get fooled: the procedure's name implies rigour on its own, but a walk-forward test refit many times on a strategy already shaped by earlier full-sample study is still measuring a strategy that has, in aggregate, seen the data it is being tested against.
Walk-forward.usage: Used to test a strategy across many rolling fit-and-test splits rather than one, so a result has to hold up over a sequence of out-of-sample windows, not just the one a researcher happened to choose.

Overfitting.long:
Overfitting is a rule set that has learned the noise in a specific dataset rather than a pattern that generalises beyond it. It happens whenever a strategy has enough free choices — parameters, filters, entry conditions — relative to the amount of independent data available to fit them.

The mechanism is capacity meeting a finite sample. Given enough adjustable pieces, a rule set can be shaped to fit almost any historical sequence closely, including its accidents. The fitted version explains the sample extremely well and the future barely at all, because the accidents it learned do not repeat.

It is often invisible from inside the fitting process: an overfitted strategy's in-sample statistics can look excellent, sometimes better than a strategy with genuine, generalising structure. The tell is not in the fit; it is in what happens when the rules meet data they were never shaped against.

Where people get fooled: more rules, more filters, and more conditions feel like progress, because each addition improves the in-sample fit. The improvement is real and almost entirely worthless — it is the strategy memorising the one history it has seen, at the expense of every history it has not.
Overfitting.usage: The default suspicion applied to any rule set with many adjustable parts and a strong in-sample result; the test is whether performance survives data and parameter settings the rules were never fitted to.

p-hacking.long:
p-hacking is adjusting an analysis after seeing preliminary results until it crosses a significance threshold — trying a different date range, a different metric, a different filter, or a different subset, and keeping whichever version passes. Each adjustment looks like ordinary refinement from the inside.

The mechanism is that every adjustment is a fresh draw against the same noise. A threshold like a five per cent significance level is calibrated for one test; run several disguised versions of the same test and keep the passing one, and the real chance of a false positive is far higher than the number printed at the end suggests.

It differs from an honest search mainly in bookkeeping and sequence: a pre-registered plan fixes the metric and criterion before results exist, while p-hacking lets the results themselves choose the metric and criterion afterward. The output can be statistically identical and epistemically opposite.

Where people get fooled: nobody sets out to p-hack. It arrives as reasonable-sounding refinement — this cut of the data is more representative, this metric is more appropriate — chosen after the fact because it happens to be the one that worked, which is exactly how noise gets mistaken for signal.
p-hacking.usage: Named as the failure mode being avoided whenever a test's parameters, metric, or sample are adjusted after an initial result is seen, rather than fixed beforehand.

Look-ahead bias.long:
Look-ahead bias is a backtest using information that would not actually have been available at the moment a trading decision was made. It is one of the most common ways a simulation quietly turns into fiction, because the leak is often a single line of code rather than a design flaw.

It shows up in familiar places: using a day's closing price to decide a trade executed earlier that day, using restated economic data as if the original release had contained the final figure, or using year-end financial statements at a date before they were actually published.

Adjusted price series are a frequent, subtle source: back-adjusting historical prices for a later stock split or dividend is standard practice, but applying today's adjustment factor to a signal computed on yesterday's bar can smuggle future information into a rule that looks perfectly ordinary.

Where people get fooled: the resulting backtest often looks unremarkable rather than absurdly good, which is what makes the bias dangerous — a small, consistent look-ahead can turn a mediocre rule into a modestly convincing one without ever producing a result implausible enough to raise suspicion.
Look-ahead bias.usage: Checked for explicitly in any backtest by tracing, line by line, whether every input to a decision was actually knowable at that decision's own timestamp.

Survivorship bias.long:
Survivorship bias is testing a strategy against only the instruments, funds, or companies that still exist today, silently excluding the ones that failed, delisted, or went bankrupt along the way. The surviving universe looks nothing like the universe an investor actually faced at the start of the period.

The mechanism is that failure is disproportionately concentrated in exactly the situations a strategy needs to be tested against — struggling companies, failed exchanges, blown-up funds. Removing them removes the downside tail from the data, so a strategy exposed to that tail is tested against a friendlier world than the one it will actually trade in.

It compounds with other filters. A track record of funds that reported five-year returns already excludes funds that closed before year five; a universe of today's top companies already excludes whatever was replaced. Each filter is individually reasonable and collectively removes the evidence of what goes wrong.

Where people get fooled: a backtest run on a clean, current list of tickers looks like ordinary due diligence, not a source of bias — the omission is invisible from inside the dataset, because the delisted names left no rows behind to notice missing.
Survivorship bias.usage: Guarded against by testing against a dataset that includes delisted and failed instruments, since a current-constituents-only universe overstates historical performance by construction.

Random-walk control.long:
A random-walk control tests whether a strategy's result is distinguishable from what a directionless, no-memory price process would have produced on its own. Simulated random-walk price paths, matched to the real market's volatility, are fed through the same strategy logic, and the real result is compared against that distribution.

The mechanism it isolates is drift and volatility that a strategy collects for free simply by being in a market that trends or by holding through calm stretches, independent of any skill in its entries or exits. A random walk shares none of the real market's structure but matches its statistical envelope.

It sits alongside, not in place of, a random trader benchmark: the random-walk control varies the market while holding the strategy logic fixed, checking whether the market's own statistical properties alone explain the result, which is a different question from whether random entries in the real market would.

Where people get fooled: a strategy that fails to beat its random-walk control is often still described as promising, when failing this control means the price series itself, with no strategy at all, already explains what was observed.
Random-walk control.usage: Run alongside a strategy backtest to check whether the result is distinguishable from what a matched, memoryless random price process would produce by itself.

Positive control.long:
A positive control is a test run against something already known to produce a real, non-zero effect, used to confirm the testing pipeline is capable of detecting one. If a method cannot recover a known effect, its failure to find a new one proves nothing about the new one.

The mechanism is separating two different failures: an idea that genuinely has no edge, and a measurement process too weak, noisy, or flawed to detect an edge that exists. Without a positive control, both look identical — a null result — and the researcher cannot tell which one occurred.

In strategy research a plausible positive control is a well-documented, previously validated effect, such as a known seasonal pattern or a factor with published academic support, run through the exact pipeline being used for new ideas. If the pipeline recovers it cleanly, a null result elsewhere carries more weight.

Where people get fooled: every failed backtest gets read as evidence the idea does not work, when a fair share of failures are the code, the cost model, or the data quietly breaking the ability to see any effect at all — a step never checked unless a positive control was run first.
Positive control.usage: Run before trusting a batch of null results, to confirm the testing pipeline can detect a known real effect before it is used to judge an unknown one.

Sample size.long:
Sample size, in a backtest, means the number of independent trades or independent time periods behind a statistic — not the number of price bars, not the length of the backtest in years, and not the number of open positions. A long history can still contain a small number of genuinely separate outcomes.

The mechanism that makes it matter is variance: per-trade outcomes carry large variance relative to any plausible edge, so small samples are dominated by luck. A thirty-trade backtest and a three-thousand-trade backtest can show the identical expectancy while deserving completely different amounts of trust.

Correlated trades shrink the effective count further. Trades that cluster in one regime, share an underlying driver, or overlap in time are not independent draws; they behave statistically like a much smaller number, and the honest sample size is the independent count, not the row count.

Where people get fooled: a large number of trades in the log is treated as automatically sufficient evidence, when the number that actually matters — how many of those trades were independent of each other — is almost always smaller, sometimes dramatically so.
Sample size.usage: Checked before trusting any backtest statistic, distinguishing the number of trades logged from the number of genuinely independent outcomes among them.

Monte Carlo.long:
Monte Carlo methods answer a question that is analytically hard to solve by simulating it many thousands of times instead. In strategy testing this usually means reshuffling a sequence of trade outcomes, resampling returns, or generating synthetic price paths, and observing the spread of results the simulations produce.

The mechanism's value is turning one historical outcome into a distribution of plausible outcomes. A single backtest produced one specific sequence of wins and losses in one specific order; a Monte Carlo resample shows how differently that same set of trades could have played out, including a different maximum drawdown or worst losing streak, purely from reordering.

The method is only as honest as what it resamples and how. Shuffling trades that are not actually independent, or generating price paths that ignore volatility clustering and fat tails, produces a synthetic world calmer and more orderly than the one being modelled, which flatters whatever is being tested.

Where people get fooled: a Monte Carlo simulation is treated as adding new information about the market, when it is really redistributing the information already in the sample — its honesty depends entirely on whether the resampling respected the dependence structure of the original data.
Monte Carlo.usage: Used to see the range of outcomes a fixed set of trades or a fitted return process could plausibly have produced, not to generate genuinely new evidence about the market.

Degrees of freedom.long:
Degrees of freedom, in strategy research, means the number of independent choices a researcher was free to make while building a rule set — parameter values, filters, entry and exit conditions, which markets and periods to include. Every free choice is a chance to fit the sample rather than the underlying pattern.

The mechanism connects to overfitting: a rule set with many degrees of freedom, tested against a finite dataset, has enough flexibility to explain that dataset's noise convincingly, much as a high-order curve can be drawn through any scatter of points without describing how those points were generated.

Degrees of freedom accumulate in places that do not look like parameters — which indicators were considered before one was chosen, the asset universe, what counts as a valid signal. Each is a decision made with knowledge of how it affects the outcome, and each spends some of the sample's evidentiary value.

Where people get fooled: only the visible, named parameters get counted. A strategy with two tunable numbers but twenty silent researcher decisions behind its final shape has far more effective degrees of freedom than its parameter count suggests, and its in-sample result is correspondingly less trustworthy.
Degrees of freedom.usage: Counted, as honestly as possible, to judge how much a rule set could have fitted its own test data rather than described something that will recur.

Benchmark.long:
A benchmark is the reference result a strategy has to beat before its own performance means anything — most commonly buy-and-hold of the same instrument or a broad market index, and a random trader matched for frequency and holding period. Without one, a positive return proves only that the return was positive.

The mechanism it isolates is opportunity cost. Capital committed to a strategy was not committed to the benchmark instead, so the relevant question is never whether this made money, but whether it made more, risk-adjusted, than the passive alternative that required no research, no monitoring, and no trading costs.

A fair benchmark has to be matched to the strategy being tested — same instrument, same period, same approximate exposure — or the comparison measures something other than skill. A strategy compared against cash, or against a benchmark from a different period, is not really being benchmarked at all.

Where people get fooled: any positive number, shown on its own, reads as success. Reported beside buy-and-hold and a random-trader control, the same number often reads very differently — which is precisely why both belong above every strategy result, not as a footnote beneath it.
Benchmark.usage: Placed above every strategy result as the passive and no-skill comparisons a strategy has to clear before its performance is treated as informative.

Cost model.long:
A cost model is the set of assumptions a backtest uses for everything trading actually costs — commission, bid-ask spread, slippage, financing on leveraged or overnight positions, and any exchange or platform fee. It converts a sequence of theoretical entries and exits into what a real account would have kept.

The mechanism that makes it decisive is that trading costs scale with turnover while edge, if it exists, is usually thin. A rule that looks profitable under a zero-cost assumption can be comfortably unprofitable once realistic costs are applied, and the higher the trade frequency, the larger that gap tends to be.

Costs are easy to understate. Spread widens in fast markets exactly when a strategy is most likely to be trading; slippage on stop orders is worse in the moves that trigger them; commission structures change with size. A cost model built from calm, liquid conditions understates what a strategy will actually pay.

Where people get fooled: a strategy's headline return is quoted before costs are named, as if costs were a minor adjustment rather than a load-bearing assumption — two researchers using the identical rule set and identical data can reach opposite conclusions purely from different cost assumptions.
Cost model.usage: Specified explicitly and conservatively before any backtest result is trusted, since the same rule set can pass or fail purely on the cost assumptions applied to it.

Latency.long:
Latency is the delay between a signal being generated and an order actually reaching the market — computation time, network transit, exchange queueing, and the time a broker takes to acknowledge and route an order. A backtest that assumes zero latency is testing a strategy that cannot exist.

The mechanism that makes it matter is that price moves during the delay. A signal computed on a closing price and assumed to fill at that same price has implicitly assumed instantaneous, costless time travel; in reality the fill happens somewhere later, at whatever price the market has moved to by then.

Latency competition is also structurally uneven. Firms invest heavily in colocation and dedicated infrastructure to shrink this delay for very short-horizon strategies, and that advantage compounds with every trade — not a gap a retail setup closes by trying harder, which is one reason very short horizons favour institutions structurally.

Where people get fooled: a backtest with same-bar fills at the signal price looks conservative because the strategy waited for a bar to close, while still quietly assuming the trade executed with no delay at all — the fill assumption, not the waiting, is where the unrealism lives.
Latency.usage: Accounted for by delaying assumed fills past the signal bar, and by treating any strategy whose edge depends on beating latency competition as outside a retail account's reach.

Vectorised vs event-driven.long:
A vectorised backtest applies a strategy's rules across a whole price series at once using array operations — fast, but structurally prone to treating every bar as visible simultaneously unless the code is written carefully to respect time. An event-driven backtest processes one bar or tick at a time, in order, mimicking how a live system actually receives information.

The mechanism-level difference is what each style makes easy to get wrong. Vectorised code makes look-ahead bias easy to introduce by accident, because a single misaligned index can let a calculation see a future value; event-driven code makes it structurally harder, at the cost of being slower to run.

Neither style is inherently more honest. A careless event-driven backtest can still leak the future through mismanaged state, and a disciplined vectorised backtest, built with explicit lags on every input, can be as clean as an event-driven one, just faster to iterate on.

Where people get fooled: speed gets equated with rigour, or its absence gets equated with safety. The style of the engine determines how easy a mistake is to make, not whether the specific backtest in front of you actually made it.
Vectorised vs event-driven.usage: A choice of implementation, not of honesty; either style needs its own explicit discipline against letting a calculation see data from the future.

Warm-up period.long:
A warm-up period is the stretch of data at the start of a backtest consumed by indicators before they produce a valid reading — a two-hundred-day moving average has nothing meaningful to say for its first two hundred days, and any trade generated during that stretch is generated from an incomplete calculation.

The mechanism it protects against is quiet contamination of the results by garbage values at the start of the series. Depending on how the code is written, an indicator with insufficient history can silently return a default or a partially computed number rather than failing loudly, and a rule built on it can generate trades that mean nothing.

The correct length of the warm-up depends on the slowest input the strategy uses — the longest lookback among all its indicators — and it should be excluded from every performance statistic, not merely from the moment trading starts, since even nearby values can still be influenced by the incomplete window.

Where people get fooled: a backtest quietly includes its warm-up period in the reported trade count or date range, padding the apparent sample size and coverage with data that was never a fair test of the strategy at all.
Warm-up period.usage: Excluded entirely from reported results and from the trade count, since indicator values computed on insufficient history are not a fair test of the rule.

Slippage model.long:
A slippage model is the assumption a backtest makes about the difference between the price a strategy's rule expects and the price an order would actually fill at. It exists because real orders move the price they touch and arrive into a market that has already moved since the signal was generated.

The mechanism that makes slippage worse than a flat, generous guess is that it correlates with exactly the conditions a strategy is most likely to trade in — fast markets, breakouts, and news releases carry both the biggest opportunities and the widest gaps between expected and achieved price, so a strategy's best-looking signals are often its worst-filled ones.

A realistic slippage model scales with volatility and order size relative to typical volume, rather than assuming a single fixed number across every condition, and it should be harshest exactly where the strategy is most eager to trade, not averaged evenly across calm and volatile periods alike.

Where people get fooled: a small, flat slippage assumption is treated as conservative because it is nonzero, while the strategies most exposed to real slippage need a model that worsens precisely when the strategy is most active, not a constant applied everywhere alike.
Slippage model.usage: Built to worsen in exactly the conditions a strategy is likely to trade in, rather than applied as a single flat number across every market state.

In-sample / out-of-sample split.long:
An in-sample and out-of-sample split divides historical data into a portion used to develop or tune a strategy and a separate portion reserved to test it, untouched, afterward. The split exists to answer one question honestly: does this rule set describe something that recurs, or only the data it was built from.

The mechanism is that any decision made while looking at data — which parameter value performed best, which filter improved results — partially fits that data's specific noise. The out-of-sample portion was never looked at during those decisions, so performance there is not inflated by the same fitting process.

The split only works while it is respected. Looking at out-of-sample results, adjusting the strategy in response, and testing again converts that data into in-sample data for the revised strategy, whether or not the researcher relabels it — the innocence of a hold-out set is spent the first time it influences a decision.

Where people get fooled: a large gap between in-sample and out-of-sample performance gets explained away as an unlucky sample or a changed market, when the far more common explanation is that the in-sample result was inflated by fitting, and the out-of-sample one is the honest reading.
In-sample / out-of-sample split.usage: The minimum structure for any strategy test: a portion of data reserved untouched until after every development decision is finalised.

Combinatorial purged CV.long:
Combinatorial purged cross-validation splits a dataset into several groups and tests many different combinations of which groups train and which test, rather than relying on one fixed train-test split. Each combination purges training observations whose labels overlap the test period, addressing the label-overlap problem specific to financial time series.

The mechanism it adds over a single walk-forward pass is coverage: instead of one sequence of rolling windows, it produces many different train-and-test partitions from the same data, each purged and typically embargoed, giving a distribution of out-of-sample results rather than a single point estimate for how a selection process performs.

The framework, developed in work associated with Marcos López de Prado, is used less to validate one final strategy and more to test the selection process itself — asking, across many partitions, how often the configuration that looked best in one split still ranks well in the others.

Where people get fooled: running the procedure feels like due diligence regardless of what feeds it. If the universe of configurations tested was already narrowed by earlier, unpurged exploration, the combinatorial structure evaluates a search that was quietly wider than the one it appears to be auditing.
Combinatorial purged CV.usage: Used to test how stable a strategy-selection process is across many different train-and-test partitions of the same data, rather than trusting the result of one split.

Anchored vs rolling walk-forward.long:
An anchored walk-forward keeps the start of the training window fixed and extends its end forward with each step, so every fit uses all history available up to that point. A rolling walk-forward instead slides a fixed-length window forward, dropping old data as new data arrives, so every fit sees roughly the same amount of history.

The trade-off is what each choice assumes about the market. Anchored windows assume older data stays relevant, which suits a slowly evolving process; rolling windows assume older data goes stale and should be discarded, which suits a market believed to shift regime over time — and either assumption can be wrong.

Anchored windows grow the effective sample size with every step, stabilising parameter estimates but slowing how fast the strategy can adapt to a genuine structural change. Rolling windows adapt faster but with a smaller, noisier sample at every step, raising the risk of refitting to short-term noise.

Where people get fooled: the choice is treated as a technical detail rather than a hypothesis about the market's stability. Testing only one of the two silently bakes in an assumption about how fast the market changes that was never itself put to the test.
Anchored vs rolling walk-forward.usage: Chosen as an explicit assumption about whether older data stays relevant or goes stale, and ideally tested both ways rather than picked by default.

Signal decay.long:
Signal decay is the tendency of a genuine trading signal to weaken over time after it becomes known or widely used, as the behaviour it exploited gets arbitraged away or the participants generating it adapt. A real edge is not guaranteed permanence even when it was once real.

The mechanism is competitive: if a signal reflects a correctable inefficiency, capital and attention flow toward exploiting it once recognised, and that flow itself erodes the opportunity — closing the gap that made it profitable. Signals sourced from a genuinely structural constraint decay more slowly than signals sourced from a correctable oversight.

Decay is hard to distinguish, in the short run, from ordinary variance. A weakening signal and a signal having an unlucky stretch produce identical-looking recent results; the difference only becomes visible over a longer horizon, or by checking whether the mechanism behind the signal is still plausibly intact.

Where people get fooled: a strategy that stops working gets treated as broken code or an irrational market, when the least dramatic explanation is usually right — the edge, if real, was never promised to last, and its slow disappearance is what a working market is meant to do to it.
Signal decay.usage: Watched for by tracking a live strategy's performance against its backtest over time, since a real edge sourced from a correctable inefficiency should be expected to weaken, not necessarily to persist.

Reproducibility.long:
Reproducibility means an independent run of the same backtest, on the same data, with the same code and settings, produces the same result. It sounds like a low bar; research pipelines routinely fail it, through undocumented data versions, hidden random seeds, or code that changed between the run and the report.

The mechanism that breaks it most often is silent state — a data file updated since the original run, a package version that changed a default, a manual step performed once and never recorded. None of these show up as an error; they show up as a slightly different number nobody can explain.

A result that cannot be reproduced cannot be checked, and a result that cannot be checked cannot be trusted, however good it looks. Reproducibility is not a courtesy for other researchers; it is the precondition for knowing whether the original result is real.

Where people get fooled: an impressive number reported once is treated as established, when an unreproduced result is closer to a claim than a finding — rerunning it from a fixed, versioned dataset and a fixed script is what turns the claim into something that can actually be relied on.
Reproducibility.usage: Verified by rerunning a backtest from fixed, versioned inputs before its result is trusted, since an unreproducible number is a claim, not a finding.

Sensitivity plateau.long:
A sensitivity plateau is a broad, flat region of parameter space in which a strategy's performance stays roughly similar across many nearby settings, rather than peaking sharply at one combination. Its presence, or absence, is one of the clearest signs of whether a strategy found a real regularity or its own best-fitted noise.

The mechanism is that a genuine pattern, driven by a real cause, tends to be robust to small changes in how it is measured — a moving average of nineteen days versus twenty-one should not flip a real trend-following effect from strongly profitable to unprofitable. A pattern appearing at one precise setting was more likely found than discovered.

Mapping the plateau means testing a grid of nearby parameter values, not just the one that scored best, and looking at the shape of performance across that grid rather than its single highest point. A narrow spike surrounded by mediocre or negative results is diagnostic on its own.

Where people get fooled: the single best-performing parameter set is reported as the strategy, while the surrounding grid that would reveal a plateau or a spike is never shown, because showing it would surface exactly the fragility a spike represents.
Sensitivity plateau.usage: Checked by testing a grid of nearby parameter values rather than just the best one, since a real effect should hold up across a range of similar settings, not one precise point.

Cost sensitivity.long:
Cost sensitivity is how much a strategy's performance changes as trading cost assumptions are varied — testing the same rule set under a range of spread, commission, and slippage figures rather than one fixed guess, to see how much of the apparent edge depends on costs staying low.

The mechanism it exposes is that a strategy's turnover determines how exposed it is to cost assumptions. A low-frequency strategy pays costs rarely, so a doubling of assumed slippage barely moves its result; a high-frequency strategy pays costs on every trade, so the identical doubling can turn a profitable backtest unprofitable outright.

Testing cost sensitivity means rerunning the backtest across a realistic range — optimistic, expected, and pessimistic cost figures — and checking whether the strategy's conclusion changes across that range, rather than reporting only the most favourable assumption available.

Where people get fooled: a single cost figure is quoted as if it were a fact about the world rather than an assumption, and a strategy that only clears its benchmark under the most optimistic end of a plausible cost range is reported as if it cleared it under realistic trading conditions.
Cost sensitivity.usage: Tested by rerunning a strategy under a range of plausible cost assumptions, since a result that only survives the most optimistic cost figure is not a robust result.

Trade clustering.long:
Trade clustering is the tendency of a strategy's trades to bunch together in time, in a single instrument, or around a single market driver, rather than being spread evenly across the sample. A hundred clustered trades carry far less evidential weight than a hundred spread-out ones.

The mechanism is shared exposure: trades that all fire during one trending quarter, one volatility regime, or one correlated basket of instruments are not independent tests of the strategy's logic — largely one test, repeated. If that one period was unusual, the whole cluster inherits its unusualness rather than averaging it away.

Clustering shrinks the effective sample size below the nominal trade count and inflates the apparent precision of statistics computed on it, because standard calculations assume independence that clustering has quietly removed. A clustered trade log can look statistically strong while resting on a handful of genuinely separate episodes.

Where people get fooled: the trade count in the log is read as the sample size, without checking whether those trades actually happened at different, unrelated times — a strategy that only ever fires during one kind of market has been tested against one kind of market, however many trades that produced.
Trade clustering.usage: Checked by looking at when and where a strategy's trades actually occurred, since trades bunched in one period or driver carry less evidential weight than the raw count implies.

Regime split test.long:
A regime split test breaks a backtest's history into distinct market conditions — trending versus ranging, high versus low volatility, rising versus falling rates — and reports a strategy's performance separately within each, rather than only as one blended average across the whole period.

The mechanism it protects against is a strategy that only works in the specific mix of regimes its backtest happened to contain. An average return computed across a trending decade and a ranging decade can look acceptable overall while concealing that the strategy loses steadily in one of the two and depends entirely on the other.

The split has to be defined honestly, ideally with rules fixed before results are examined, since defining regimes after seeing which subperiods flatter the strategy is a way of smuggling a favourable cut into the test — the same hazard multiple testing creates elsewhere.

Where people get fooled: a single blended headline number is treated as describing the strategy, when it may really describe a strategy that performs acceptably in one regime and destructively in another, with the average simply hiding which is which — a distinction that matters to anyone holding it through a regime change.
Regime split test.usage: Run by reporting performance separately across defined market regimes, since a single blended average can hide a strategy that depends on one type of market and loses in every other.

Paper-to-live gap.long:
The paper-to-live gap is the difference between a strategy's simulated or paper-traded performance and what it actually achieves once real capital and real execution are involved. Even a perfectly honest backtest and paper record can fail to predict live results, because paper trading still omits certain frictions that only appear with real money.

The mechanism includes execution effects a simulation struggles to capture — fills competing with other market participants, slippage under real order-book depth, psychological pressure changing whether rules are actually followed under a live losing streak, and capital constraints on position sizing that a spreadsheet ignores.

The gap also has a behavioural half: a rule followed mechanically in a backtest is not automatically followed by a person watching their own capital move in real time, so part of the gap between paper and live performance can be the strategy failing to be executed as specified, not the strategy itself failing.

Where people get fooled: a strong paper-trading record is treated as proof the strategy is ready for live capital, when paper trading validates the mechanics and the logic, not the discipline, execution quality, or emotional load of doing it with money that can actually be lost.
Paper-to-live gap.usage: Expected by default rather than treated as a sign something went wrong, since paper performance omits frictions and behavioural pressure that only appear once real capital is involved.

Strategy capacity check.long:
A strategy capacity check estimates how much money a strategy can absorb before its own trading starts moving prices against it, eroding the edge a smaller test never had to contend with. A backtest run at a hypothetical size says nothing about performance at the size actually intended.

The mechanism is market impact: an edge measured on historical prices assumes the strategy's own trades did not influence those prices, realistic only when position sizes are small relative to typical volume. Scale the rules up and the strategy's own footprint starts working against it, degrading fills exactly where the backtest assumed none.

Capacity is not fixed — it depends on liquidity, holding period, and how patiently the strategy can execute. A slower strategy with a longer holding period generally tolerates more capital than a fast one competing for the same fills, because it can spread its footprint over more time.

Where people get fooled: a backtest's percentage returns are assumed to scale linearly with capital, when a strategy's real capacity is often far below the size an investor wants to deploy — an edge genuine at small size can simply not exist at the size someone wants it to fund.
Strategy capacity check.usage: Estimated before scaling a strategy with more capital, since an edge measured at a small hypothetical size is not guaranteed to survive the price impact of a much larger one.

Data snooping.long:
Data snooping is drawing conclusions from a dataset after having already explored it — trying multiple hypotheses, metrics, or subsets against the same data until something interesting turns up, then presenting that finding as if it had been anticipated. The data gets consulted for ideas and then asked to validate them.

The mechanism is that repeated exploration of a fixed dataset accumulates the same false-positive risk as any other form of multiple testing, whether or not each individual look felt like a formal test. Twenty casual glances at the same data, each searching for something worth pursuing, carry roughly the statistical burden of twenty formal hypothesis tests.

It is distinct from ordinary exploratory analysis mainly in what happens next: exploration becomes snooping specifically when a pattern noticed during that exploration is then reported, without adjustment, as if it had been confirmed on fresh evidence rather than discovered by looking.

Where people get fooled: the exploratory phase feels informal and undocumented, so it does not feel like it counts — but the dataset does not distinguish a formal grid search from a researcher's intuition wandering over the same numbers; both spend the data's ability to confirm anything new.
Data snooping.usage: Guarded against by treating any pattern noticed while exploring a dataset as a hypothesis to be tested on separate, untouched data, never as a finding in its own right.

Regime change.long:
A regime change is a structural shift in how a market behaves — a change in volatility level, correlation structure, trend persistence, or policy and liquidity backdrop — that makes the statistical relationships a strategy was built on no longer hold the same way.

The mechanism that makes it dangerous is that regimes are usually visible only after they end. A strategy built during a low-volatility, trending period encodes assumptions specific to that period, and nothing in a standard backtest flags them as period-specific — they simply look like the rules until the regime that produced them ends.

Regime change is one reason a long backtest is not automatically a strong one: a longer history gives more scope for regimes to differ within it, and averaging performance across several different regimes can obscure that a strategy depended on only one of them.

Where people get fooled: a strategy that stops working gets diagnosed as broken or decayed, when the more accurate description is often that the market it was built for stopped existing — a distinction that matters, because it changes whether the fix is retuning the strategy or accepting a period-specific pattern was never a durable edge.
Regime change.usage: Named as one honest explanation, alongside overfitting, for why a strategy's live results diverge from its backtest, since the market that generated the backtest may no longer be the market being traded.

Stationarity.long:
Stationarity is the statistical property of a process whose defining characteristics — mean, variance, the way values relate to their own past — stay constant over time. Most standard statistical tools quietly assume it. Financial return series are, to varying degrees, not stationary, and the degree matters more than the label.

The mechanism is that volatility, correlations, and even the sign of expected drift shift across market regimes, so a statistic fitted on one stretch of history is implicitly a description of that stretch's particular, temporary character rather than a universal law the market obeys going forward.

Some transformations improve matters without solving it entirely — returns behave more stationarily than raw prices — but volatility clustering and regime shifts mean even return series drift in their properties over long horizons, which is why techniques built for stationary data need adjustment before use on markets.

Where people get fooled: a statistic — a correlation, a volatility estimate, a fitted relationship — computed on historical data is treated as a fixed property of the market, when it is really a snapshot of one non-stationary process that may already be behaving differently by the time the number is used.
Stationarity.usage: Kept in mind whenever a statistic fitted on historical data is applied forward, since markets are not fully stationary and a relationship measured in the past is not guaranteed to hold at the same strength going forward.

Bootstrap.long:
The bootstrap builds an estimate of uncertainty by resampling a dataset with replacement many times and recomputing a statistic on each resample, using the spread of those recomputed values as a stand-in for the sampling variability that would otherwise require repeating the original experiment many times over.

Its usefulness in strategy research is that it needs no assumption about the underlying distribution of returns — unlike formulas that assume normality, the bootstrap works directly with whatever shape the actual data has, which matters given how far real return distributions sit from normal.

The ordinary bootstrap assumes each observation is independent, which financial time series violate through volatility clustering and serial dependence. Resampling single days at random destroys that structure, producing confidence intervals narrower and drawdown estimates gentler than reality — the block bootstrap exists specifically to preserve it by resampling contiguous chunks instead of single points.

Where people get fooled: a bootstrapped confidence interval looks rigorous simply by being computational rather than a rule-of-thumb, but an ordinary bootstrap applied to dependent market data quietly manufactures false precision — the method's honesty depends entirely on whether the resampling respects the dependence the original series actually has.
Bootstrap.usage: Used to estimate the uncertainty around a backtest statistic without assuming a particular return distribution, provided the resampling method respects any dependence in the data.

Bonferroni correction.long:
The Bonferroni correction adjusts the significance threshold a result must clear to account for how many tests were run to find it — dividing the standard threshold by the test count, so a search of a hundred variants demands a result far less likely to arise from chance before being called significant.

The mechanism it corrects for is the arithmetic of repeated testing: running many independent tests against the same threshold makes at least one false positive close to certain, regardless of whether any real effect exists among them. The correction restores the original, intended false-positive rate for the whole search, not one isolated test.

It is a conservative correction — simple to apply, but strict enough to miss real effects when tests are correlated, since it assumes the worst case for how much each test adds to false-positive risk. Less conservative alternatives exist, but they trade away some of that safety margin.

Where people get fooled: a p-value is judged against the standard threshold regardless of how many variants were searched to produce it — the correction is the reminder that the bar rises with the search, not stay fixed at the level appropriate for a single, pre-registered test.
Bonferroni correction.usage: Applied to raise the significance bar a result must clear in proportion to how many variants were tested to find it, citable by name whenever a search's size needs to be priced into its winner's credibility.

Deflated Sharpe ratio.long:
The deflated Sharpe ratio adjusts a strategy's measured Sharpe ratio downward to account for how many trials were run to find it, how long the track record is, and the skew and fat-tailedness of its returns, producing a figure that answers whether the observed Sharpe is distinguishable from the best of many noisy attempts.

The mechanism is that selecting the best-performing configuration out of many candidates biases its Sharpe ratio upward — the winner of a search is, in part, the luckiest entrant. The deflation, developed in work by Bailey and López de Prado, estimates and removes that inflation given the number of trials involved.

A short track record and heavily skewed or fat-tailed returns both widen the plausible range a Sharpe ratio could have arisen from by chance, so the same raw Sharpe deflates by different amounts depending on how much data backs it and how well-behaved that distribution is.

Where people get fooled: a raw Sharpe ratio is quoted as if it were self-evidently meaningful, when the same number can represent either a genuinely strong strategy or the accidental winner of a wide, unrecorded search — the deflated version is what tries to tell those two apart.
Deflated Sharpe ratio.usage: Cited by name, after Bailey and López de Prado, as the correction that answers whether a strategy's Sharpe ratio is distinguishable from the best result of the trials that produced it.

Point-in-time data.long:
Point-in-time data preserves exactly what was known and published as of each historical date, rather than the modern, revised, or backfilled version of the same series. Economic figures get revised after release, index constituents change, and financial statements get restated — point-in-time data keeps the original vintage attached to its date.

The mechanism it defends against is a specific, easy-to-miss form of look-ahead bias: using today's revised GDP figure, today's index membership list, or today's restated earnings as if that information had existed on the historical date being tested, when market participants at that date only had the original, unrevised numbers.

Point-in-time data is harder to obtain and maintain than ordinary historical data, because most data providers only keep the latest version of each series, overwriting the vintage that would have been visible at the time — the honesty this data type provides has to be actively sourced, not assumed.

Where people get fooled: a backtest using standard historical prices feels rigorous because the price series is genuinely historical, while the supporting data feeding its signals — economic releases, fundamentals, index membership — is quietly the current, revised version, smuggling foresight into a test that otherwise looks clean.
Point-in-time data.usage: Required for any signal built on economic, fundamental, or index-membership data, since the current, revised version of that data was not available on the historical dates being tested.

Parameter sensitivity.long:
Parameter sensitivity is how much a strategy's performance changes as its parameter values are nudged away from whatever setting scored best. Measuring it means testing a range of nearby values, not just the winning one, and looking at how sharply the result degrades as the setting moves.

The mechanism connects directly to overfitting: a strategy with high sensitivity, where a small change in one parameter flips the result from strongly profitable to unprofitable, has likely found a setting fitted precisely to the noise of the test data, since a genuine underlying pattern is rarely so exactly tuned to one specific number.

Low sensitivity, where a broad range of nearby settings all perform similarly, is more consistent with a real, generalisable effect, though it is not proof of one — a robust-looking plateau can still reflect a spuriously robust pattern if the underlying data itself is limited or unusual.

Where people get fooled: only the single best parameter combination is reported, with no picture of how the surrounding grid behaves — a strategy whose performance collapses one step away from its optimum in either direction is being presented as if that fragility were a virtue rather than a warning.
Parameter sensitivity.usage: Tested by scanning a grid of nearby parameter values rather than reporting only the best-performing setting, since sharp sensitivity to small changes is a common signature of overfitting.

Live decay.long:
Live decay is the gap that opens between a strategy's backtested or paper performance and its performance once actually trading live, growing over time as more live data accumulates. It differs from a single bad stretch by persisting and widening rather than reverting toward the backtest's numbers.

The mechanism can be any combination of honest causes: the edge weakening through signal decay as others exploit it, a genuine regime change making the historical pattern less relevant, execution and cost realities the backtest underestimated, or the original backtest having been overfitted and never containing a real edge to begin with.

Distinguishing these causes matters because they call for different responses — a decayed edge or a changed regime argues for retiring or rebuilding the strategy, a cost or execution shortfall argues for fixing the implementation, and an originally overfitted backtest argues there was nothing to decay from at all.

Where people get fooled: live decay gets treated as a rough patch to be waited out, on the assumption the backtest numbers are the true performance the strategy will return to, when for many strategies the backtest number was always the outlier, and the decaying live result is the more accurate estimate.
Live decay.usage: Tracked by comparing live results against the backtest on a rolling basis, treated as informative from the first divergence rather than dismissed until it becomes severe.

Portfolio heat.long:
Portfolio heat is the sum of risk exposed across every open position at once — not any single trade's risk alone, but what the account stands to lose if every open stop were hit at once. A trader risking a disciplined amount per trade can still carry undisciplined total heat.

The mechanism that makes it different from position-level risk is correlation. Five positions each risking one per cent, in unrelated instruments, really do cap combined loss near five per cent. The same five positions correlated can move together, so one event hits several stops at once — the per-trade risk was honest, the combined exposure was not.

Heat also changes through the trade: a position moved to break-even no longer contributes to heat while still open, while a new position added on top of existing ones raises it at once — heat has to be tracked live, not assumed from the entry plan.

Where people get fooled: risk discipline is measured trade by trade, at one or two per cent each, while combined exposure across open, correlated positions is never added up — the account can be one move away from a loss well beyond what any single figure implied.
Portfolio heat.usage: Tracked as the total risk live across every open position at once, particularly when those positions are correlated, rather than assessed one trade at a time.

Defined risk.long:
Defined risk means the maximum possible loss on a position is known and fixed in advance, structurally — not through intention to exit at a point, but because the position's own construction caps the loss. A long option, for instance, cannot lose more than the premium paid, regardless of what the underlying does.

The mechanism distinguishes it from a stop-loss order, which expresses an intention to exit at a level but does not guarantee the exit happens there — a gap, a halt, or a fast market can fill the stop well past the intended level, so a stop defines an intended loss, not a structural one.

Defined-risk positions typically cost something for that certainty — an option's premium, a spread's width — the trade-off against positions with no structural cap on loss: cheaper to establish, but exposed to a loss with no hard ceiling, particularly under gaps or illiquid conditions.

Where people get fooled: a stop order gets described as if it capped risk the way an option or a spread does, when a stop only expresses an intention — the market has to actually let the order fill near the stop price, and it does not always oblige.
Defined risk.usage: Used to describe a position whose maximum loss is capped by its own structure, as distinct from a stop order, which only expresses an intended exit the market may not honour.

Hedge.long:
A hedge is a position taken to offset the risk of another position, accepting a cost or a capped upside in exchange for reduced downside if the hedged risk materialises. Its purpose is risk reduction, not profit, even though a hedge can individually make or lose money.

The mechanism only works to the extent the hedge is genuinely negatively correlated, or structurally opposite, to the exposure being protected. A hedge chosen for convenience rather than for how it behaves can fail to protect exactly when needed most, during a stress event that breaks the usual relationship between the two.

Hedges have a cost, whether an explicit premium, a give-up of upside, or ongoing carry, and that cost is the price of reduced variance, not a flaw — judging a hedge by whether it made money misses that its job was to lose a little, reliably, in exchange for not losing a lot occasionally.

Where people get fooled: correlations that hold in calm markets often shift or invert during genuine stress, which is precisely when a hedge is being relied upon — a hedge validated only against ordinary market conditions has not really been tested against the conditions it exists for.
Hedge.usage: Assessed by whether it reduces the variance of the combined position across a range of scenarios, not by whether the hedge itself was profitable on its own.

Position limit.long:
A position limit is a hard cap on how much can be committed to a single instrument, sector, or correlated group, set in advance and enforced regardless of how confident a particular trade idea feels in the moment. Its function is to bound the damage any one mistaken belief can do.

The mechanism it defends against is conviction itself. The trades that breach sensible limits are rarely careless ones — they are usually the ideas that felt most certain, which is exactly when an account is most tempted to override its own rules, and exactly when being wrong does the most damage.

A limit set at the instrument level alone can still be breached in substance by several correlated instruments each individually within their limit — a real position limit has to account for correlated exposure, treating a cluster of related positions as contributing to the same cap rather than as separate allowances.

Where people get fooled: a limit that can be overridden in the moment is not really a limit, it is a suggestion — the discipline only holds when the cap is decided before conviction is high, and followed precisely when conviction argues loudest for an exception.
Position limit.usage: Set in advance, before any specific trade idea exists, precisely because the trades most likely to breach it are the ones that feel most convincing at the time.

Break-even stop.long:
A break-even stop is a stop-loss moved to the entry price once a trade has moved favourably, converting a position that could lose money into one that, if stopped out from there, loses nothing beyond transaction costs — a common way to manage a trade after an initial profit.

The mechanism worth understanding is what it removes and what it does not: it removes the risk of the original loss, but it does not remove exposure to further adverse movement before the stop is reached, and it forecloses any chance the trade recovers from a dip that would have gone on to work.

Moved too early, a break-even stop can convert an ordinary, expected pullback into an unnecessary exit at zero, turning what the plan treated as normal noise into a stopped-out trade — the timing of the move matters as much as the mechanic itself.

Where people get fooled: moving a stop to break-even feels like pure risk reduction with no downside, when it is really a trade-off — capped downside from here in exchange for a higher chance of being stopped out of a position that would have worked, on a retracement the plan was built to tolerate.
Break-even stop.usage: Applied deliberately, at a point consistent with the trade's own volatility, rather than reflexively at the first sign of profit, since moving it too early raises the chance of exiting a trade that would have gone on to work.

Time stop.long:
A time stop closes a position after a fixed amount of time regardless of price, on the reasoning that a trade thesis is meant to play out within some expected window, and a position hitting neither its target nor its stop by then has arguably already told the trader something.

The mechanism it captures is that capital and attention have a cost even when a position is not losing money. A trade sitting flat far longer than its thesis anticipated ties up risk budget and mental bandwidth better used elsewhere — not yet wrong is not the same as still working.

A time stop needs a horizon set from the trade's own logic — a specific catalyst, or a typical holding period for the setup — rather than an arbitrary number, since an unrelated limit on a genuinely slow-developing thesis can exit a trade before it had any real chance to work.

Where people get fooled: a position with no price-based reason to exit gets held indefinitely on the assumption that not losing means still valid, when a thesis producing no progress within its timeframe has usually already failed in substance, even while the stop has not yet been touched.
Time stop.usage: Set from the trade's own expected timeframe at entry, so a position that has produced no progress within that window is treated as informative, not merely as not-yet-wrong.

Kelly fraction in practice.long:
The Kelly criterion computes the position size that maximises the long-run growth rate of capital, given a genuinely known edge and payoff distribution. The Kelly fraction in practice is the recognition that trading rarely supplies either input with confidence, and full Kelly sizing punishes being wrong.

The mechanism that makes full Kelly dangerous is that its formula is highly sensitive to the inputs, and those inputs — win probability, payoff ratio — are estimates from a finite, noisy sample, not known constants. An overestimated edge fed into it produces an oversized position, and sizing errors compound because they scale with capital.

The common response is fractional Kelly — sizing deliberately at some fraction, often a half or a quarter, of what the formula recommends — sacrificing some theoretical growth rate for far less sensitivity to estimation error and a shallower drawdown if the edge estimate turns out optimistic.

Where people get fooled: the Kelly formula is treated as a precise prescription because it comes from mathematics, when its output is only as reliable as the edge estimate fed into it — an estimate drawn from backtest statistics that are themselves uncertain, often inflated by the search that found the strategy.
Kelly fraction in practice.usage: Applied, when used at all, at a deliberately reduced fraction of the formula's output, because the edge estimate feeding the calculation is itself uncertain and full Kelly punishes an overestimate severely.

Fixed fractional sizing.long:
Fixed fractional sizing risks a constant percentage of current account equity on each trade, rather than a constant dollar amount. Position size therefore shrinks automatically after losses and grows automatically after gains, tracking the account's actual capital rather than staying fixed against a balance that has moved.

The mechanism this produces is a built-in brake during losing streaks: because each loss is a percentage of a smaller account, consecutive losses cost progressively less in absolute terms, which slows the rate of capital destruction compared with risking a fixed dollar figure that does not adjust as the account shrinks.

The same mechanism works in reverse during winning streaks, compounding position size upward as equity grows — which increases long-run growth potential if the edge persists, but also means a reversal after a strong run risks a larger absolute amount than the trader was risking at the start of that run.

Where people get fooled: the percentage figure, say one per cent per trade, is treated as a fixed, safe number regardless of context, when the same percentage applied to a much larger account after a winning streak represents a much larger absolute risk than the trader originally calibrated for.
Fixed fractional sizing.usage: Used to size positions as a percentage of current equity rather than a fixed dollar figure, which shrinks risk automatically during losing streaks and grows it automatically during winning ones.

Anti-martingale.long:
An anti-martingale approach increases position size after wins and decreases it after losses, the opposite of a martingale, which increases size after losses to recover faster. The logic is to press size when a strategy is, in some sense, currently working, and pull back when it is not.

The mechanism's appeal is that it avoids the martingale's structural flaw: escalating bets after losses require, mathematically, unlimited capital and no position limits to guarantee eventual recovery, a condition no real account satisfies, which is why a losing streak can wipe out a martingale account rather than merely dent it.

An anti-martingale trades that safety for a different exposure: sizing up after a winning streak concentrates more capital right at the point a reversal, if one is coming, does the most damage — it protects against ruin from a losing streak but not against giving back a large fraction of recent gains.

Where people get fooled: anti-martingale sounds like the safe, disciplined alternative by contrast with its dangerous namesake, when it is really a different risk profile, not a risk-free one — capital is still concentrated after a run of wins, right before any reversal that logic never ruled out.
Anti-martingale.usage: Named as the practice of sizing up after wins and down after losses, distinguished from martingale sizing by avoiding ruin from a losing streak, not by avoiding the risk of giving back gains after a winning one.

Sequence risk.long:
Sequence risk is the fact that identical returns, earned in a different order, produce different account outcomes whenever money is added to or withdrawn along the way. Two return streams with the same average and total return can leave very different final balances, purely from the order the returns arrived in.

The mechanism is arithmetic: a withdrawal taken from a smaller account, after early losses, permanently removes more of the account's future compounding capacity than the same withdrawal taken from an account that grew first — an early loss, before withdrawals compound the damage, is costlier than the identical loss arriving later, after gains built a larger buffer.

The same mechanism runs in reverse for deposits, and it matters most during retirement drawdowns or funded-account payout schedules, where cash leaves on a schedule the trader does not control and cannot simply wait out the way an accumulation-only investor could.

Where people get fooled: two strategies with identical average returns and identical volatility are treated as equivalent, when the order those returns arrive in, relative to when money is added or withdrawn, can leave one account intact and the other severely depleted, from arithmetic alone, with no difference in underlying skill.
Sequence risk.usage: Considered whenever withdrawals or deposits happen alongside trading, since the order returns arrive in changes the outcome even when the average return and volatility are identical.

Sortino ratio.long:
The Sortino ratio measures risk-adjusted return using only downside volatility in its denominator, rather than total volatility the way the Sharpe ratio does. Upside variability is not the risk an investor minds — only variability below some target return, usually zero, is the risk being managed against.

The difference matters most for asymmetric return distributions — a strategy with frequent small gains and rare large gains has high total volatility from the upside surprises alone, and a Sharpe ratio penalises that even though nobody experiences a large unexpected gain as a risk. The Sortino ratio does not penalise it.

Because it uses only half the distribution, the Sortino ratio is computed from fewer data points than the Sharpe ratio for the same sample, which makes it noisier and more sensitive to a small number of downside observations — a single bad tail event can move it more than a total-volatility measure.

Where people get fooled: a strategy is chosen because its Sortino ratio looks stronger than its Sharpe ratio, without checking why — sometimes it reflects a favourable, asymmetric return shape, and sometimes a downside sample too thin to estimate reliably, which the ratio itself does not disclose.
Sortino ratio.usage: Read alongside the Sharpe ratio rather than in place of it, and interpreted with attention to how few downside observations the denominator was actually computed from.

Calmar ratio.long:
The Calmar ratio divides a strategy's annualised return by its maximum drawdown, giving a single figure that answers how much return was earned per unit of the worst peak-to-trough loss experienced. It is a return-to-pain measure built around the drawdown investors tend to find most difficult to sit through.

The mechanism that makes it useful alongside volatility-based ratios is that maximum drawdown captures a path-dependent risk that standard deviation can miss — two strategies with identical volatility can have very different maximum drawdowns depending on whether losses were spread out or concentrated into one severe stretch.

Its weakness is that it is built from a single historical event, the one worst drawdown in the sample, rather than a distribution of outcomes, so it is highly sensitive to sample length and to whether that period happened to contain an unusually severe or mild stress episode.

Where people get fooled: a strong Calmar ratio from a short backtest reads as evidence of resilience, when a short sample may simply not yet contain the stress event that would reveal a much larger drawdown — the ratio only reports the worst thing that has happened so far, not the worst thing that can.
Calmar ratio.usage: Read with attention to how much history the maximum drawdown was drawn from, since a short or fortunate sample can flatter the ratio by simply not yet containing a worse stress period.

Compounding.long:
Compounding is earning returns on previous returns, not just the original capital — basic enough to underrate, and the reason losses and gains are not symmetric the way casual arithmetic suggests. A given percentage loss requires a larger gain to recover, from the shrunken base the gain works from.

The mechanism is straightforward: a fifty per cent drawdown leaves half the capital remaining, and that half needs to gain one hundred per cent, not fifty, just to return to the starting balance. Required recovery rises faster than the loss deepens, which is why large drawdowns are disproportionately dangerous to compounding.

The same mechanism rewards consistency over intensity: a strategy compounding a modest, steady expectancy without severe drawdowns tends to outperform, over long horizons, one with a higher average return interrupted by deep losses, since deep losses cost more to recover from than they cost to create.

Where people get fooled: a fifty per cent loss and a fifty per cent gain are treated as roughly offsetting because the numbers look symmetric, when compounding makes them nothing of the kind — the account needs double the gain to recover, which is why avoiding large drawdowns matters more than chasing large gains.
Compounding.usage: The reason a percentage loss and the equal percentage gain that reverses it are not equivalent — the required recovery grows faster than the loss, which is why avoiding deep drawdowns compounds more value than chasing occasional large gains.
